notes: \cpara{Opens with Hastorf and Cantril's study of a rough Dartmouth-Princeton game (1954). The percentages match the paper's table.}

\cfact{The sentence's contrast, 86\% against ``only 36\%,'' is sharper than the table's. The students chose among ``Dartmouth started it,'' ``Princeton started it,'' ``Both started it'' and ``Neither.'' The 36\% blamed Dartmouth alone; the 53\% who answered ``Both,'' as the parenthesis says, also blamed Dartmouth, so 89\% of Dartmouth students blamed their own team at least in part, against 97\% of Princeton students. For the same reason, ``Nearly everyone agreed that Princeton hadn't started it'' is true only of Princeton alone, which 2\% and 0\% chose. The paper puts it this way: ``the majority of Dartmouth students thought both sides were to blame.''}

\cpara{Reports the film test correctly: 4.3 against 9.8 Dartmouth infractions, and the paper's ratios of ``flagrant'' to ``mild,'' about one to one for Dartmouth viewers and two to one for Princeton viewers, give ``half'' and ``a third.''}

\cpara{States the general claim, that thoughts and perceptions defend what we value, and adds a hypothesis, marked as held by ``some psychologists.'' The summary fits Mercier and Sperber's abstract: ``Skilled arguers, however, are not after the truth but after arguments supporting their views.''}
\cpara{Summarizes work on confabulation and introspection, hedged with ``often'' and ``can.'' I did not check the three works cited.}
\cpara{Asks how we can reach a realistic view of the world and of our own minds, when our thinking about thinking is also suspect.}
\cpara{Offers mathematics as the model: axioms for arithmetic gave a standard for judging answers.}
\cpara{Extends the model: probability theory formalizes rational belief, and decision theory rational action.}
\cpara{Says that, given priors and evidence, probability theory fixes the best new beliefs ``uniquely and precisely.'' That is correct as stated, since the priors are taken as given.}
\cpara{Sets up the example: one of six classmates is a secret admirer, with no reason to favor any of them.}
\cpara{Gives the prior odds, 1:5, which is correct.}
\cpara{Rules out ``fifty-fifty'' and says 1:5 follows from the assumptions. Footnote 8 calls one of them unrealistic.}
\cpara{Adds the evidence: people with a crush wink ten times as often, and Bob winks.}

\clogic{Loosely worded. ``Ten times as often'' is a likelihood ratio, as the paragraph after next calls it. It is not the odds that a random person who winks at you has a crush on you; those also depend on how many people have one. Reading a likelihood ratio as those odds is the base rate neglect described in ``Biases: An Introduction.''}
\cpara{Warns against the opposite error, treating the evidence as settling the question.}
\cpara{Multiplies the odds: 1:5 times 10:1 gives 10:5, or 2:1, a probability of 2/3. The arithmetic is right.}

\cpara{The introduction's central claim: ``given very modest constraints,'' the question of what to believe ``has an objectively right answer,'' and ``There is always a correct amount of confidence.'' The Bob example has one because it fixes its inputs: six equally likely candidates and a known ratio of ten. Consistency alone does not fix a prior, and Bayesians are divided on whether anything else does. In the words of the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}, subjective Bayesians ``hold that every prior is permitted unless it fails to be coherent.'' The introduction states one side of that dispute as settled. Our notes on ``How Much Evidence Does It Take?'' make the same point about starting probabilities.}
\cpara{Contrasts this with talk of beliefs as a matter of taste, and introduces Robin Hanson.}
\cpara{Quotes Hanson's 2006 post ``You Are Never Entitled to Your Opinion.'' The quoted words match it.}

\cpara{Restates the claim above without its condition, ``Given our assumptions'': the answer about Bob is ``just as logically constrained'' as an answer in algebra. See the note on the objectively right answer.}
\cpara{Grants that humans are no more perfect reasoners than perfect calculators. Footnote 10 adds that even an ideal reasoner in the real world must approximate.}
\cpara{Argues that the ideal still guides improvement and shows where we went wrong.}
\cpara{Compares learning rationality without a framework to memorizing sums, and states the book's purpose: to help readers build such frameworks.}
\cpara{Gives the book's origin in Yudkowsky's blog posts.}
\cpara{Places this book second of six.}
\cpara{Quotes Scott Alexander's 2014 post; the words match it.}
\cpara{Says rationality helps most where evidence is limited or read through biases.}
\cpara{Says the same rules apply to personal life, politics and debates about technology, so the book ranges widely.}
\cpara{Introduces the first sequence, on questions where the odds are extreme. The paragraph ends in an ellipsis in the LessWrong text.}
\cpara{Introduces Politics and Rationality with two questions: why political disputes feel so personal, and why importance does not make us more careful.}
\cpara{Answers, hedged with ``hints,'' that much reasoning is rationalization, and names two more sequences.}
\cpara{Introduces Death Spirals, on hazards for groups built around shared ideas, and the last sequence, Letting Go.}
\cpara{Grants that we do not naturally reason like Bayesians, and that reciting the axioms would not change what the students saw.}
\cpara{Quotes Luke Muehlhauser's 2011 post; the words match it.}
\cpara{Says biases are the substance of our reasoning, not an addition to it. The quotation is the only support.}

\cpara{Answers that debiasing is still possible, by analogy with arithmetic, which can be trained. As in ``Biases: An Introduction'' (see the notes there), the claim that debiasing is possible is supported by an analogy, with no evidence that teaching of the book's kind achieves it.}
\cpara{Names two assumptions of the example that are unrealistic.}
\cpara{Says that even an ideal reasoner in the real world must use approximations.}
